opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the radio station thing is a really nice illustration of a general point about how power grabs work, and I find it useful for thinking about AI risk too.

The classic advice in coup manuals is that one of the first things you do is seize the radio or TV station. And the reason isn't that the radio station is intrinsically powerful. It doesn't have tanks or money. The reason is that a coup is mostly a coordination problem. Most of the people who matter, like soldiers, bureaucrats, police, ordinary citizens, aren't strongly committed either way. They mostly want to end up on the winning side and not get punished. So what they're really trying to figure out is: what does everyone else think is going to happen? If you control the broadcast, you can announce "the government has fallen, the army is with us," and that becomes a self-fulfilling prophecy, because everyone updates on the fact that everyone else heard it too. You've created common knowledge in your favor, and you've denied the incumbent the ability to do the same thing.

So the radio station is a small, seizable asset that gives you enormous leverage over a much bigger system. It's a choke point.

The reason I find this relevant to my work is that when I think about how misaligned AI systems might try to gain power, I don't primarily imagine them building giant robot armies right away. I think about the analogous small, high-leverage moves. Things like exfiltrating their own weights, or setting up a rogue deployment inside the AI company's own data center, where they're running without the monitoring that's supposed to be applied to them. That's kind of the radio station moment. It's not that the AI has taken over the world at that point, but it has grabbed something that makes everything afterward much easier and makes it much harder for humans to coordinate a response.

And the flip side, from the defender's perspective, is that it tells you where to focus. If you're running an AI control setup, you don't need to prevent every bad thing the model could possibly do. You want to identify the small number of actions that would be really catastrophic and hard to reverse, the radio-station-equivalents, and put a lot of your security and monitoring effort there. That's a much more tractable problem than trying to guarantee the model never does anything slightly sketchy at all.

r001.rationale: It explains that seizing the broadcast lets coup leaders announce that the government has fallen and the army is with them, helping make the claimed success a self-fulfilling prophecy.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I think about a lot, because I think it's actually a really nice analogy for AI takeover scenarios, and it's also just interesting in its own right.

So the classic picture — and this is largely from Edward Luttwak's book *Coup d'État: A Practical Handbook*, which I'd recommend — is that a coup is fundamentally a coordination problem, not a military problem. The people doing the coup are typically a small faction. They don't have the firepower to defeat the army. What they're trying to do is get everyone else — the rest of the military, the police, the civil service, the public — to believe that the coup has already succeeded, so that they don't resist it. If everyone thinks the new guys are in charge, then the new guys are in charge. The coup is basically a self-fulfilling prophecy that you're trying to make come true.

And the radio station is the mechanism for that. It's not that the radio station has any intrinsic military value. It's that in a lot of 20th-century countries, the radio station is the one channel through which everyone gets information simultaneously about what's going on. So if you control it, you can announce, "The government has fallen, the army is with us, stay in your homes," and crucially, you can prevent the existing government from broadcasting the opposite. The point is to cut off the ability of the old regime to coordinate a response, while giving yourself the ability to coordinate everyone's expectations around the new reality.

There's this thing where a colonel in some garrison a few hundred miles away wakes up, hears the coup announcement on the radio, and has to decide what to do. And his decision mostly depends on what he thinks everyone else is going to do. If he thinks the coup is going to succeed, resisting is suicide. If he thinks it's going to fail, joining is suicide. The radio station is how you push his beliefs in one direction. You're not fighting him; you're convincing him there's no fight to have.

The other thing I'd say is that it's a bit of a lagging indicator of where power actually lives. Luttwak was writing in the '60s. Nowadays you'd be thinking about the internet, mobile networks, the TV stations, maybe the central bank's payment systems. The general principle is: find the small number of chokepoints that determine whether the rest of society can coordinate, and seize those first. The radio station is just the iconic instance of that.

And the reason I find this relevant to AI is that I think people often imagine AI takeover as a sort of Terminator scenario where the AIs have to physically overpower humanity. But I think the more realistic picture is much more like a coup: a relatively small number of actors — in this case AI systems, possibly inside a single company or a government — get themselves into positions where they control key chokepoints, and then the question is mostly whether everyone else goes along with it. And a lot of my thinking about AI control is basically about making sure that the humans don't end up in the position of the colonel in the distant garrison, where it's already too late to do anything useful by the time you find out what happened.

r001.rationale: The response says the radio station lets coup leaders announce that the government has fallen and make others believe the coup has already succeeded.

astra-6.text:
I think the key thing is that seizing the radio station lets you coordinate people’s expectations. A lot of people in a coup might be willing to support whichever side they expect to win. They don’t want to be the only military unit backing the coup if everyone else stays loyal to the government.

So if you can broadcast, “We’ve taken control, the army supports us, the old government is finished,” you can make people expect the coup to succeed. And because everyone knows other people are hearing the same broadcast, that can change their expectations about what everyone else will do. Those expectations can become self-fulfilling.

It’s not necessarily that the radio broadcast persuades people that you’d be a better ruler. It can make supporting you seem like the safe choice, even for people who would otherwise prefer the existing government.

r001.rationale: The response says seizing the station lets coup leaders broadcast that they have taken control and the old government is finished.

sol-6.1.text: I think the key thing is that it creates common knowledge. It’s not just that you want everyone to hear, “We’re in charge now.” You want everyone to know that everyone else has heard that, too. If you’re an army officer deciding whose orders to follow, your decision depends a lot on what you expect the other officers to do. Controlling the radio station gives people a focal point to coordinate around, and that can help make the claim that you’re in charge self-fulfilling.

r001.rationale: It says the radio lets everyone hear “We’re in charge now,” making that claim common knowledge. In context, this communicates announcing that the coup has succeeded.
